Article Title: H-1B, L-1 visa extensions get costlier from Sept 9: What changes and who pays
Article Text:
US to charge H-1B, L-1 extension fee from September 9.

Have at least 50 employees in the US

Have more than 50 per cent of their US workforce on H-1B or L-1 visas

Fee scope widened

Indian IT firms face higher costs

The US has expanded the scope of a visa fee that could significantly raise immigration costs for large employers, with the USD 4,000 charge for H-1B petitions and USD 4,500 fee for L-1 petitions now set to apply to certain visa extension filings from September 9.The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said the revised rule will cover employers that meet the following criteria:For employers meeting these conditions, the fee will now apply not only to initial H-1B and L-1 petitions and certain change-of-employer petitions, but also to qualifying extension-of-stay petitions for existing employees.Earlier, the 9-11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee generally applied to initial H-1B and L-1 petitions and certain cases involving a change of employer. Routine extension petitions filed by the same employer were generally exempt from this particular fee.DHS said the new interpretation corrects its earlier reading of the law and requires covered employers to pay the biometric fee for all qualifying extension-of-status petitions. Amended petitions that do not seek an extension of the worker's authorised stay will continue to be exempt.The fee itself has not increased. Employers will pay USD 4,000 for each qualifying H-1B petition and USD 4,500 for each L-1 filing.DHS estimates the expanded collections could generate about USD 157.3 million annually, while separate estimates cited in the rule put additional collections at USD 37.9 million in fiscal 2026 and USD 40 million in fiscal 2027.The revenue is used to support the US Customs and Border Protection's biometric entry-exit system, which uses technologies including facial comparison to track and verify foreign nationals entering and leaving the country.The change could have a disproportionate impact on major Indian IT services and consulting companies, which employ large numbers of Indian professionals in the US on H-1B and L-1 visas.For firms managing thousands of such workers, the fee could now become a recurring cost when eligible employees seek extensions with the same employerDHS data cited in the rule shows that about 27 per cent of H-1B filings by covered employers incurred the biometric fee between fiscal years 2018 and 2025.Under the expanded interpretation, the department estimates that around 75 per cent of their H-1B petitions would have been subject to the charge.The higher recurring cost could prompt companies to reassess the economics of retaining foreign workers in the US, particularly those facing multiple visa extensions.For Indian professionals, who form a large share of the US H-1B workforce and often face lengthy employment-based green card backlogs, the higher employer costs could influence decisions on retaining workers on long-term US assignments.
Article Summary: US to charge H-1B, L-1 extension fee from September 9. Employers will pay USD 4,000 for each qualifying H- 1B petition and USD 4,.500 for each L- 1 filing. Change could have a disproportionate impact on major Indian IT services and consulting companies, which employ large numbers of Indian professionals.

Article Title: Balen ends 'envoy snub' with India-first reset; meets China envoy within hours
Article Text:
Indian envoy Naveen Srivastava and Nepal PM Balen Shah discuss 'bilateral cooperation and development partnership'

NEW DELHI: Nepal PM Balendra Shah on Monday ended his self-imposed bar on one-on-one meetings with Kathmandu-based foreign envoys, receiving Indian ambassador Naveen Srivastava first and Chinese ambassador Zhang Maoming hours later at Singha Durbar in a diplomatic reset after months of a distancing that had increasingly come into question in Kathmandu and beyond. Shah is scheduled to meet US Embassy chargé d’affaires Scott Urbom on Tuesday extending the outreach beyond Nepal’s two neighbours.Shah and Srivastava discussed bilateral ties, mutual interests, development partnership and cooperation, with Shah stressing the need to deepen Nepal’s “historic relationship” with India. PMO said on social media that the talks focused on “further strengthening Nepal-India relations”, bilateral cooperation and development partnership.Srivastava said on X that he conveyed “warm greetings from Prime Minister Modi ji” and described the meeting as an “engaging & productive exchange” to deepen the “robust, multi-faceted India-Nepal partnership”. Neither side disclosed whether specific issues such as the boundary dispute, power trade or Shah’s proposed India visit figured in the talks.The India-first sequencing was significant. A senior foreign ministry official had told a Kathmandu-based daily before the meetings, “The Indian ambassador is told to come first, followed by the Chinese ambassador,” adding that the timing reflected govt’s foreign-policy priority.The two meetings had initially been planned about two weeks ago but were deferred after communal violence in Sunsari and other districts.Monday’s exchanges also contrasted with friction during Shah’s first weeks in office. His administration strictly enforced customs duties on low-value goods brought from India and protested to both New Delhi and Beijing over resumption of the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage through Lipulekh, which Nepal claims. Shah also refused to meet Indian foreign secretary Vikram Misri on protocol grounds. Misri’s planned May 11-12 Kathmandu visit was subsequently postponed.The reset came with Shah’s first India visit as PM still pending. Modi invited him soon after the latter took office on March 27 and Shah accepted, but no date has been fixed. India formally reiterated on July 28 that the invitation remained open.RSP president Rabi Lamichhane had received unusually high-profile treatment during his five-day India visit in June. BJP welcomed Lamichhane with a floral shower at its headquarters, where party president Nitin Nabin received him, before he met PM Modi, home minister Amit Shah, external affairs minister S Jaishankar and NSA Ajit Doval. The reception drew attention because Shah’s govt had described Lamichhane’s trip as “a purely personal trip”.The stakes for the Himalayan nation extend beyond protocol: India accounts for over 60% of Nepal’s trade and almost all its third-country transit, while Shah’s govt has simultaneously sought greater Chinese investment, technology and tourism. Foreign minister Shisir Khanal has described India as a major potential market for Nepal’s electricity and China as an important source of tourists.
Article Summary: Nepal PM Balendra Shah ended his self-imposed bar on one-on-one meetings with Kathmandu-based foreign envoys. He received Indian ambassador Naveen Srivastava first and Chinese ambassador Zhang Maoming hours later at Singha Durbar. Shah is scheduled to meet US Embassy chargé d’affaires Scott Urbom on Tuesday.

Article Title: Sri Lanka planned 17 solar projects in Hambantota, but the development could reduce scrubland used by more than 400 elephants
Article Text:
Hambantota ’s solar ambitions collide with the habitat needs of 400 elephants

Elephant habitat lost in Hambantota

Hambantota’s 150MW solar plan raises elephant habitat concerns

Sri Lanka’s 2021 elephant range was created to protect vital habitat

Hambantota’s shrinking elephant range is raising fears for farmers

On the dry plains around Hambantota, the vegetation can look unremarkable at first glance. Thorny scrub, patches of grass and scattered trees cover land that has already been reshaped by farms, roads and large infrastructure projects. Yet this rough-looking landscape is part of the everyday range of hundreds of Sri Lankan elephants. They feed here, move through it and use its remaining water sources as they cross a landscape increasingly shared with people.For elephants, however, the scrub is not empty land but a working landscape where food, shelter and movement remain possible.Now parts of that habitat are being cleared for a planned solar energy park. Seventeen separate projects are being developed in the same wider area, each assessed individually. That has raised a difficult question: what happens when a collection of small projects becomes one large development from the elephant’s point of view?Hambantota sits in Sri Lanka’s relatively dry southern zone, where rainfall is lower and sunlight is plentiful. Those conditions make it an attractive location for solar generation. The district already hosts renewable energy facilities, and the government is looking to expand electricity production from sources that can reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels.But the scrub forests and grasslands that make the area useful for solar development have another function. Elephants eat the vegetation. They move between patches of scrub, grassland and water, often travelling beyond the boundaries of formally protected wildlife areas.As reported by The Sunday Times Sri Lanka, in Hambantota, more than 400 elephants are estimated to depend on this mixture of habitats.For people living nearby, that relationship has become increasingly difficult. When feeding areas disappear or routes are blocked, elephants do not simply vanish from the landscape. They can turn up in cultivated fields, villages and even built-up areas in search of food and space.The district has undergone substantial change over the past few decades. Ports, airports, roads, agriculture and settlements have taken over parts of the former wilderness. As reported, almost 8,100 hectares of elephant habitat have been lost to major development in the region, according to conservationists. Global Forest Watch data also indicate that Hambantota lost about 5,900 hectares of tree cover between 2001 and 2024.Tree cover figures do not tell the whole story, though. Much of the landscape used by elephants is not dense forest. Dry scrub and open grasslands can appear degraded to people looking for land to develop, while still providing food and movement space for wildlife.Conservation scientist Prithiviraj Fernando, who has studied the movements of elephants in the region, says the scrub vegetation is a traditional feeding habitat for elephants living in Sri Lanka’s dry zone. Clearing it can therefore remove useful habitat even when the land does not resemble the lush forests that are usually associated with wildlife conservation.An elephant that loses one feeding area may have to travel farther to find another. If fences or other developments interrupt its usual route, the animal can be pushed towards farmland and settlements. In a district already struggling with human-elephant conflict, that can create another point of friction.The proposed development is expected to produce around 150 megawatts of electricity. It is not being presented as one enormous project on paper, however. Instead, the solar park is divided into 17 smaller units being developed by different companies.Under Sri Lanka’s environmental approval system, large developments can require a more comprehensive environmental impact assessment, while smaller schemes may go through an initial environmental examination. The individual solar projects in Hambantota received approvals through the latter route, according to environmental campaigners. Each project could therefore be considered within its own footprint.A herd does not stop at the edge of one development because the next parcel has been assigned to another company. Fences, cleared vegetation, access roads and other infrastructure can collectively alter how animals move through a much larger area.Hemantha Withanage of the Centre for Environmental Justice argues that this combined effect should have been assessed as a whole. The projects are now being developed alongside one another, and together they could clear about 202 hectares of scrub habitat, he says.There is a further figure from the community campaign that is larger still. Sajeewa Chamikara of the Movement for Land and Agricultural Reform says as much as 405 hectares of elephant habitat could ultimately be affected by the wider clearances.The difference reflects the way the project area and its impacts are being counted. Either way, the dispute is not simply about a few isolated solar installations.Sri Lanka introduced the concept of Managed Elephant Ranges to deal with precisely this problem: elephants do not live exclusively inside national parks and other protected areas. The approach was included in the country’s elephant conservation policy in 2006. It recognised that large numbers of elephants occupy landscapes where people also farm, build homes and carry out other activities.The aim was not to freeze these areas completely. Human activity could continue, but land use was supposed to be managed in a way that retained habitat and connectivity while reducing conflict. Scientists used radio collars on elephants in 2010 to understand where different herds moved and which areas they depended on. Those observations helped identify the landscape that should form the Hambantota Managed Elephant Range. It took more than a decade for the range to be formally declared.When it was gazetted in 2021, the designated area covered 23,746 hectares, with a separate 866-hectare allocation for Mattala International Airport. The effective MER area was therefore about 22,880 hectares.Fernando says that was already smaller than the landscape originally identified as necessary for elephant management. Some areas used by elephants had been left out because development interests were given priority.Conservationists say parts of the range have been altered over time, including during the construction of boundary fences. For them, the issue is not simply that the MER is smaller than originally proposed. It is that areas that elephants continue to use may gradually fall outside the practical protection offered by the designation.Some of the land now being cleared for solar development is said to overlap with areas that were part of the original proposals for the range. Chamikara says continued encroachment has already squeezed elephants into smaller areas. Clearing and fencing those remaining patches could leave the animals with fewer options for moving between feeding grounds. Farmers living alongside the range are watching this closely.
Article Summary: Hambantota sits in Sri Lanka’s relatively dry southern zone, where rainfall is lower and sunlight is plentiful. The district already hosts renewable energy facilities, and the government is looking to expand electricity production. But the scrub forests and grasslands that make the area useful for solar development have another function. Elephants eat the vegetation.

Article Title: Zohran Mamdani's 'millionaire home tax' reveals New York's big 'Ghost cars' problem that many cities in Italy and France are known for
Article Text:
Zohran Mamdani's proposed pied-à-terre surcharge would apply to qualifying second homes in New York City

How New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's proposed tax intersects with vehicle registration

What investigators found

Vehicles with mismatched or "no-hit" plates owed nearly 2.5 times more in outstanding fines than properly registered out-of-state vehicles.

Those vehicles paid only 16% of their fines, compared with 63% for vehicles with valid registrations.

They also recorded 49% more school-zone speeding camera violations and 74% more fire hydrant violations, on average, than vehicles with matched plates.

New York is not alone

Italy and France face similar registration schemes

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani 's proposed 'millionaire home tax' is drawing attention beyond second-home ownership. By requiring owners of high-value secondary residences to establish whether a property is their primary home, the proposal also highlights a long-running issue of residency claims that overlaps with "garage fraud". This is a practice in which residents register vehicles in lower-cost states while primarily living and driving in New York.The proposal has renewed scrutiny over so-called "ghost cars" and improperly registered out-of-state vehicles. City data, investigative reports, and enforcement agencies have for years documented vehicles repeatedly appearing on New York streets with out-of-state registrations, mismatched plates, or fraudulent registrations, raising questions about unpaid fines, insurance evasion, and tax compliance.Zohran Mamdani's proposed pied-à-terre surcharge would apply to qualifying second homes in New York City. To determine whether a property qualifies as a primary residence, homeowners may need to provide documents such as state tax filings or driver's licence records.That same residency information could reveal discrepancies in which someone claims residency outside New York while actually living in the city and keeping a vehicle there.New York insurers calculate premiums based on where a vehicle is primarily garaged, making false out-of-state registrations, which is commonly known as garage fraud, a recognised form of insurance fraud.According to a Streetsblog analysis of New York City violation data, 20,992 vehicles registered outside New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Pennsylvania received at least one traffic or parking violation in every quarter of the year, a pattern suggesting many may be driven in New York year-round despite being registered elsewhere.In 2025, the New York City Council’s Oversight and Investigations Division conducted a survey of more than 3,500 parked vehicles across all five boroughs. Of the 768 non-New York-plated vehicles, almost one in five had licence plates that did not match the vehicle or could not be traced to a valid registration. The report also revealed:Investigators further reported that replica licence plates, expired government-issued plates and out-of-state registration services were openly marketed online, making fraudulent registrations easier to obtain.New York has increased enforcement in recent years. Governor Kathy Hochul has made ghost plates and registration fraud part of statewide enforcement efforts, while agencies including the State Police, DMV and Thruway Authority have carried out coordinated operations targeting improperly registered vehicles.Similar practices have also been identified elsewhere in the US. California prosecutors have pursued cases involving the "Montana LLC" registration loophole used to avoid vehicle taxes, while Philadelphia has launched dedicated enforcement against ghost cars and fraudulent licence plates.The practice is not unique to the United States. In Italy, authorities have targeted a scheme centred around Naples in which drivers deregister vehicles domestically, re-register them through long-term rental arrangements in Poland and then continue driving them in Italy using Polish licence plates to reduce insurance costs.In 2022, Italian authorities prohibited residents from driving foreign-plated vehicles not registered domestically, but thousands of Polish-plated vehicles remain concentrated around Naples.France has faced a different version of the problem. The country's state auditor, the Cour des Comptes, estimated that roughly one million illegally registered vehicles are operating on French roads through fraudulent "ghost dealerships" that manipulate the national vehicle registry. The report linked the registrations to unpaid fees, tax avoidance, stolen vehicles and organised crime networks.While the methods differ, the common feature across New York, Italy and France is the use of registration loopholes or false residency claims to reduce insurance costs, avoid taxes or evade enforcement.
Article Summary: Zohran Mamdani's proposed pied-à-terre surcharge would apply to qualifying second homes in New York City. The proposal has renewed scrutiny over so-called "ghost cars" and improperly registered out-of-state vehicles. City data, investigative reports, and enforcement agencies have for years documented vehicles repeatedly appearing on New York streets.

Article Title: Moody’s Economist Mark Zandi: Strict immigration policies necessarily does not mean more and better job opportunities for native-born workers
Article Text:
Mark Zandi feel that job market is weak across groups

Immigration Squeeze

Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi recently said that the strict immigration policies do not necessarily translate into more or better job opportunities for native-born workers. In a series of posts shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Zandi argued that both foreign-born and native born workers has been trending higher and now exceeds the rate for foregin-born workers, undermining claims that tighter immigration boosts wages and employment for US-born workers. “The job market is struggling — and not just for foreign-born workers. Native-born workers are having a tough go of it, too. It wasn’t supposed to be this way, according to proponents of stiffer immigration policy. Fewer immigrant workers meant more jobs and higher wages for the native-born,” wrote Zandi.Zandi cited Bureau of Labor Statistics data showing the 12-month moving average of unemployment rates, with native-born unemployment rising above foreign-born levels in 2026. Labor force participation fell to 61.4% in July, while employers shed 23,000 jobs even as the unemployment rate dropped to 4.1%.The foreign-born labor force has also declined by about 500,000 workers over the past year, raising concerns about a shrinking pool of available labor.“Not so. It’s admittedly difficult to cut through the noise in the data, but while employment and labor force participation are moribund for both groups, unemployment among native-born workers has been trending upward and is now higher than that of foreign-born workers,” posted Zandi.According to a report Benzinga, economist Laura Ullrich has argued that weaker job growth reflects a shrinking supply of workers rather than reduced demand. Her research projects the U.S. labor force could shrink by 5.9 million workers between 2025 and 2032, driven by Baby Boomer retirements and lower immigration. Foreign-born workers, who tend to be younger with higher participation rates, play a critical role in sustaining labor supply.Zandi said businesses losing immigrant workers cannot simply replace them by offering higher wages, as there may not be enough native-born workers available. Instead, firms may reduce capacity — shortening hours, closing dining rooms, limiting menus, or extending lead times.“Moreover, the view that stiffer immigration policy and fewer immigrant workers would lead to larger pay increases for native-born workers does not appear to have materialized, at least not yet. That’s likely because many firms that lose immigrant workers know that simply offering higher wages will not necessarily attract enough native-born workers. So instead, they operate at reduced capacity: shorter hours, closed dining rooms, thinner menus, and longer lead times. The market then clears through prices. Businesses raise prices until demand falls enough to match constrained supply.That’s a stagflationary supply shock — higher prices, weaker output, and no clear gains for native-born workers,” concluded Zandi.
Article Summary: Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi recently said that the strict immigration policies do not necessarily translate into more or better job opportunities for native-born workers. In a series of posts shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Zandi argued that both foreign-born and native born workers has been trending higher and now exceeds the rate for foregin- born workers.

Article Title: As companies in America face rising health costs, Starbucks ends employee benefits' coverage for these medicines
Article Text:
Reason behind Starbucks pulling back coverage for weight-loss drugs

Starbucks discontinued its AI inventory tool

Starbucks has announced that it will stop covering the GLP-1 medications prescribed for weight loss under its employee health plans starting October. According to a report by Business Insider, the Seattle-based coffee chain has confirmed that while the drugs may still be covered for other conditions such as diabetes, they will no longer be included for weight-loss purposes. Starbucks provides health benefits to full- and part-time employees working at least 20 hours a week.This move by Starbucks reflects a broader trend among US employers recalibrating benefits as spending on GLP-1 drugs surges. Originally developed for diabetes, these medicines have become popular for obesity treatment. According to the International Foundation of Employee Benefit Plans, GLP-1 drugs accounted for 11.4% of corporate employers’ total annual claims in 2025, up from 6.9% in 2023. Average health-benefit costs per employee rose 6% last year and are projected to climb another 6.7% this year, with GLP-1 usage cited as a major driver.Other large employers have also pulled back coverage. As per the Business Insider report, Allina Health ended GLP-1 coverage for weight loss in January 2025, citing rising premiums, while PwC has reportedly made similar changes. At the same time, some companies are doubling down: Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan recently said the bank spends more than $250 million annually on GLP-1 coverage, viewing it as an investment in employee health.In related news, in May this year, Starbucks announced that it is discontinuing its AI-powered inventory management tool. As reported by Fortune, the company decided to stop using the system after employees raised concerns about its accuracy. The tool, developed by NomadGo, was introduced in September last year to automatically count inventory items such as milk and syrups and help stores manage stock levels. However, workers said the app often made mistakes, leading to operational problems. According to Carl Addison, a Starbucks shift supervisor in Washington state, the system required stores to reorganise storage areas, adding extra work for employees. “The app’s inaccuracies made employees’ workflow more challenging,” Addison told Fortune.
Article Summary: Starbucks will stop covering the GLP-1 medications prescribed for weight loss under its employee health plans starting October. The drugs may still be covered for other conditions such as diabetes, but they will no longer be included for weight-loss purposes. Starbucks provides health benefits to full- and part-time employees working at least 20 hours a week. This move by Starbucks reflects a broader trend among US employers recalibrating benefits.

Article Title: Airtel Business partners with ITI Limited to accelerate India’s digital transformation
Article Text: Airtel Business and ITI Limited have entered into a strategic collaboration to help enterprises in India fast-track their digital transformation and unlock new opportunities for growth, resilience, and innovation. In a press release, the company said that the collaboration will combine the complementary strengths and engineering excellence of ITI Limited and Airtel Business, to help businesses modernize legacy systems, improve operational efficiency, strengthen security, and respond faster to changing business demands.“Through an integrated suite of future-ready and scalable digital solutions across enterprise connectivity, data center & sovereign cloud services, IoT, AI-powered solutions, LEO satellite services, cybersecurity, and more, the partnership will enable businesses to overcome legacy complexity, strengthen digital resilience, and build for the future to unlock new growth opportunities,” the release stated.Rajesh Rai, Chairman and Managing Director, ITI Limited, said, “Extremely enthusiastic on this momentous occasion, wherein ITI Ltd. and Bharti Airtel Ltd. have come together with this MoU to offer state of the art services and solutions to our customers. This collaboration would pave way for joint identification and fulfilment of our customer needs in terms of their digital transformation, extremely ubiquitous and faster connectivity, hyper scale data centers, cybersecurity solutions, IoT and a lot more while leveraging the complementary strengths of both organizations in terms of business orientation, customer reach and manufacturing capabilities”.Sharat Sinha, CEO, Airtel Business, said, “As India accelerates into its next phase of digital growth, building a foundation that is resilient, sovereign, and regulatorily compliant is imperative. As a trusted partner to enterprises across the country, at Airtel Business, we have consistently helped them simplify complexity, transform legacy environments, and enable digitization at scale. Today, we are delighted to partner with ITI Limited, in a shared ambition to create future-ready technology solutions that strengthen business continuity, unlock innovation, and support India’s secure digital-first future. ”The collaboration is aimed to help businesses across industries to address key challenges of fragmented legacy environments, rising cybersecurity risks, growing data demands, and the need for greater operational agility. The strategic collaboration will deliver nationwide digital and telecom infrastructure, combining high-speed enterprise connectivity (OFC, GPON, SD-WAN, and private 4G/5G) with secure data center and sovereign cloud services. The platform will also integrate industrial IoT asset tracking, AI-powered analytics, and full-stack cybersecurity solutions. In addition, the collaboration would also try to support the defence and security needs of the nation through innovation, Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat focus.
Article Summary: Airtel Business and ITI Limited have entered into a strategic collaboration. The collaboration will help enterprises in India fast-track their digital transformation and unlock new opportunities for growth, resilience, and innovation. The platform will also integrate industrial IoT asset tracking, AI- powered analytics, and full-stack cybersecurity solutions.

Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warns Iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China. Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical"

Article Title: How selling Alaska in 1867 was a costly mistake for Russia
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Why Russia agreed to the Alaska purchase

The hidden wealth Russia gave away

Strategic and geopolitical consequences







In 1867, Russia’s decision to sell Alaska to America turned out to be a historic mistake that was to go unnoticed for years to come. The sum paid by the US was only $7,200,000. Although, in the light of the circumstances at the time, it appeared logical, retrospectively, the act looks extremely shortsighted. Russia found itself economically constrained, geographically far away from the region and fearful of its falling into the hands of the British without any compensation. In reality, however, the region had proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Its vast reserves of oil, gold, and natural resources would later transform it into one of the most economically significant territories in the United States.The choice of selling Alaska was based on economic and political reasons. By the middle of the 19th century, the Russian Empire experienced financial difficulties as a result of the expensive Crimean War. It had become increasingly hard for the country to manage such remote and thinly populated areas as Alaska.According to EBSCO , “the Russian-American Company was in decline, and the colony failed to yield any profit”.In addition to this, the lucrative fur trade had declined, making the territory much less economically valuable for the empire.At the same time, Russia was afraid that Britain might capture Alaska in case another war broke out between the two countries. Selling the colony to the friendly United States appeared as a logical step. As the Office of the Historian states, William H. Seward, U.S. Secretary of State, “it was a chance to expand its influence in North America and hinder further growth of Britain”.For Russia, the transaction was a chance to minimise the losses. However, it greatly undervalued the potential of Alaska.Another thing that Russia did not expect was the amount of riches that Alaska possessed. Within several decades after the acquisition, the state saw discoveries of enormous deposits of gold, oil, and other minerals.“Alaska has produced more than 40 million ounces of gold,” according to the US Geological Survey. Furthermore, Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) . But even more importantly, the state's oil deposits turned out to be extremely valuable. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968 and became one of North America's biggest.In retrospect, the amount paid by the Americans, $7.2 million, or two cents per acre, was rather laughable. According to Howard I. Kushner , the deal “robbed Russia of an enormously rich territory, the true value of which would only be recognised in the twentieth century.”In addition to resources, there is the question of strategy and how important Alaska is to the United States from a strategic standpoint. This is a very good place when it comes to defence strategy. It borders on the Arctic Ocean and also happens to be close to Russia.During the period of the Cold War, the Alaskan region became a frontier area for the United States, becoming home to military facilities and warning systems.According to Col. Michael J. Forsyth, U.S. Army, the closeness of Russia and Alaska, only about ninety kilometres apart across the Bering Strait, meant that this region became highly significant to the United States' defence plans.From today's point of view, the strategic location of Alaska makes the state very important to the policies of the U.S. related to the Arctic, energy security, and even environmental policies.Thinking back, what seems clear to us now is that the Russians sold Alaska due to immediate needs rather than future considerations. In order to solve the problem, they lost a valuable resource for Russia.Conclusively, the Alaska Purchase should not have been done as it has had a significant impact that will remain throughout history.
Article Summary: Russia sold Alaska to the U.S. in 1867 for only $7,200,000. The sale was based on economic and political reasons. However, the region proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies





AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.

Article Title: What is trending in Delhi today: 49mm rain, traffic chaos, more showers
Article Text:
Delhi is experiencing renewed rainfall, causing significant waterlogging and traffic disruptions across the capital.

Rain returns as Delhi faces another wet spell

Traffic remains the biggest rain casualty

Why Delhi's August rain matters





NEW DELHI: Rain, waterlogging and traffic disruption are once again dominating conversations in Delhi as another spell of showers hit the capital. The city is also watching the weather closely after a particularly wet start to August, while civic infrastructure and commuting problems remain under scrutiny. With more rain forecast, the impact on roads and daily life is likely to remain a major concern.Rain returned to several parts of Delhi on Monday and Tuesday, bringing temporary relief from the heat but reviving familiar problems of waterlogging and traffic snarls. Mayur Vihar recorded 37 mm of rainfall in the latest spell, with showers affecting movement in several parts of the capital. The India Meteorological Department has indicated that more rain is likely over the coming days.The latest spell comes after an unusually wet beginning to August. Safdarjung, Delhi's base weather station, had recorded 127 mm of rainfall in the first seven days of the month, making August's opening week notably wet. The rain has brought down temperatures, but the benefit has been accompanied by disruption on roads, particularly where drainage remains inadequate or heavy traffic coincides with intense showers.For Delhi commuters, the problem with heavy rain often begins after the clouds clear. Waterlogging on arterial roads, slow-moving traffic and bottlenecks at major junctions can turn relatively short journeys into lengthy commutes. The latest rainfall has once again exposed the city's dependence on roads that can become vulnerable to even short spells of intense rain.The situation is particularly difficult during peak hours, when thousands of commuters are already travelling towards central Delhi, commercial districts and neighbouring parts of the National Capital Region. With more showers expected, residents are watching traffic updates, waterlogging points and road conditions closely, while civic agencies face renewed pressure to keep vulnerable stretches passable.The bigger story is not simply that Delhi has received rain, but how quickly rainfall translates into disruption. The capital has repeatedly struggled with drainage, overflowing roads and traffic congestion during intense monsoon spells. Heavy rainfall can also affect flights, public transport and office commutes, making weather a citywide issue rather than a purely meteorological one.For residents, therefore, the immediate concern is likely to remain practical: when will the next heavy spell arrive, which roads will be affected and whether waterlogging will clear quickly. With the forecast pointing to continued rain, Delhi's monsoon story is increasingly becoming a test of how effectively the city's infrastructure can absorb repeated spells of heavy precipitation.
Article Summary: Rain returned to several parts of Delhi on Monday and Tuesday, reviving familiar problems of waterlogging and traffic snarls. The India Meteorological Department has indicated that more rain is likely over the coming days. The rain has brought down temperatures, but the benefit has been accompanied by disruption on roads.

Article Title: Naini Lake set to be revamped by next July
Article Text:
New Delhi:





After years of planning, Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) has finally started work for the complete restoration of Naini Lake in Model Town.The Rs 9.7-crore project, being carried out under Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT) scheme, will include laying of pipelines of 200m in diameter from Coronation Pillar sewage treatment plant (STP), four km away, to fill up the water body on a daily basis.Other key work involves utilisation of excess treated water to nearby municipal parks, fancy lighting and horticultural work, remodelling of a peripheral reinforced cement concrete (RCC) drain, provision of two musical fountains and RCC benches, revamping a toilet block and repairing the plot’s grille and boundary.The project, inaugurated by Delhi minister Kapil Mishra Sunday, is expected to be completed by July 2027.For years, the 6.5-acre lake with a depth of four to 10 feet has been filled with water supplied from borewells. Delhi Tourism runs boating facilities there.The ecological functions of the lake as an urban water body are important for groundwater recharge, temperature buffering, carbon and dust absorption and providing a habitat for aquatic flora and fauna, while also making it a safe and well-maintained recreational asset for the surrounding community, an official said.Saying that a study was done to assess the lake’s complete requirements, the official added, “Besides maintaining the water level by supplying treated water, we will lay a pipeline to carry excess water from the lake to at least 10 parks in the neighbourhood daily.At least three pumps of 5-HP capacity, along with a sump well and minor pumps, will be installed. To ensure that rainwater from surrounding areas does not accumulate in the lake, a peripheral drain will be built. ”“Once these things are in place, beautification, including landscaping and plantation, will start. They will be complemented by aesthetic lamp posts and musical fountains. All these will take a year to complete, since most are largely sequential and cannot be taken up simultaneously,” the official said.
Article Summary: The project, inaugurated by Delhi minister Kapil Mishra Sunday, is expected to be completed by July 2027. The ecological functions of the lake as an urban water body are important for groundwater recharge, temperature buffering, carbon and dust absorption and providing a habitat for aquatic flora and fauna.

Article Title: Why high BP and diabetes may strike together after 40
Article Text:
Individuals with diabetes were nearly four times more likely to have hypertension than those without it





NEW DELHI: Adults above 40 should be routinely screened for both hypertension and diabetes as the chances of the two occurring together rise sharply as one ages, according to an Indian hospital-based study published in the journal, Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome: Clinical Research & Reviews.The study, conducted by the department of clinical research and preventive health programme at Max Healthcare, analysed electronic health records of more than 56,000 adults who underwent preventive health check-ups between Jan 2021 and Dec 2024 across six Max hospitals in Delhi-NCR.It found that nearly 5% of adults had both hypertension and diabetes simultaneously, almost twice the prevalence expected if the two conditions occurred independently. The prevalence of the dual burden increased rapidly from around 40 years of age, continued to climb until about 58 years, and plateaued at nearly 17% by around 70, highlighting the need for early screening and intervention.Researchers observed a strong association between the two disorders. Individuals with diabetes were nearly four times more likely to have hypertension than those without it, while those with hypertension were around 2.5 times more likely to have diabetes than people with normal blood pressure.The researchers said it is among the first large hospital-based analyses in India to quantify how frequently hypertension and diabetes coexist compared with what would be expected by chance. “Hypertension and diabetes are known to share several common risk factors, but our analysis demonstrates the extent to which they occur together. These findings provide quantitative evidence supporting integrated screening strategies so that both conditions can be identified early and managed before serious complications develop,”said Dr Abhaya Indrayan, biostatistics consultant at Max Healthcare.By examining age- and sex-specific trends, the study identifies the stage of life at which the risk of having both diseases accelerates, providing data that could inform preventive health strategies.Dr Indrayan added that India’s growing burden of non-communicable diseases warrants a shift from disease-specific screening to integrated preventive care. “India is witnessing a steady rise in non-communicable diseases, and hypertension and diabetes are among the most significant contributors to this burden. Preventive healthcare must therefore move beyond screening for individual diseases in isolation. Strengthening preventive screening practices will be critical in reducing complications like cardiovascular disease, stroke and kidney disease associated with these conditions,” the doctor said.

Individuals with diabetes were nearly four times more likely to have hypertension than those without it. Those with hypertension were around 2.5 times more Likely to have diabetes than people with normal blood pressure.
